nodes.name: Big bluestem
nodes.desc: A tall dominant prairie grass. The MDC says prairie species such as prairie-chickens and Henslow's sparrows indirectly depend on it, and it is excellent forage for livestock.

nodes.name: Indiangrass & switchgrass
nodes.desc: Tall warm-season grasses that grow alongside big bluestem.

nodes.name: Little bluestem
nodes.desc: A shorter bunchgrass of drier prairie ground.

nodes.name: Prairie wildflowers
nodes.desc: Coneflowers, rosinweeds and many other flowering plants that feed pollinators and browsers.

nodes.name: Milkweed
nodes.desc: A prairie wildflower whose nectar feeds butterflies. The MDC lists Mead's milkweed as a prairie species at risk.

nodes.name: American bison
nodes.desc: The MDC says historically vast herds disturbed the prairie in ways that helped maintain it. Today only small managed herds remain.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: Browses wildflowers and young plants. Wikipedia notes its droppings spread nutrients that support plant diversity.

nodes.name: Grasshoppers
nodes.desc: Chew grasses and wildflowers all summer and feed birds, badgers and many other predators.

nodes.name: Regal fritillary
nodes.desc: A butterfly the MDC names among the species that cannot persist without prairie. Adults feed on nectar from flowers such as milkweed and coneflower.

nodes.name: Eastern cottontail
nodes.desc: Eats grasses and wildflowers and is prey for hawks, coyotes and bobcats.

nodes.name: Prairie vole
nodes.desc: A small grass-eating rodent and a staple for hawks, harriers, coyotes and badgers.

nodes.name: Thirteen-lined ground squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats seeds and insects, hibernates, and is a main prey of badgers and hawks.

nodes.name: Greater prairie-chicken
nodes.desc: Eats seeds, fruit, green plants and insects such as grasshoppers. Wikipedia says Missouri once held hundreds of thousands but only about 500 remain, and that the MDC is bringing birds in from Kansas and Nebraska.

nodes.name: Dickcissel
nodes.desc: A grassland songbird that nests in prairie and eats insects and seeds.

nodes.name: Henslow's sparrow
nodes.desc: A secretive sparrow the MDC says cannot persist without big bluestem prairie. Eats insects and seeds.

nodes.name: Red-tailed hawk
nodes.desc: Hunts voles, ground squirrels, rabbits and birds from perches over open ground.

nodes.name: Northern harrier
nodes.desc: Glides low over the grass hunting voles and small birds.

nodes.name: American badger
nodes.desc: Digs out ground squirrels, pocket gophers and other rodents. Wikipedia lists snakes, ground-nesting birds and insects as other prey.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: Ambushes rabbits, rodents, birds and young deer along woodland edges.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Today's top predator of the prairie. Eats rabbits, rodents, birds and fawns.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Warm-season grasses grow fastest in summer heat.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Rain falls mostly in spring and early summer and sets how tall the grass grows.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Fire clears dead growth and keeps trees from taking over. Wikipedia and the MDC both describe prairies as fire-adapted.

nodes.name: Deep prairie soil
nodes.desc: Dense roots hold the soil, with big bluestem roots saturating the top two feet and reaching about twelve feet deep, per the MDC.

nodes.name: Fungi, earthworms & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead grass and dung and return nutrients to the soil.
